title: UDP and the sockets API
goal: By the end you can read a UDP header, write a UDP client and server in Kotlin with timeouts, say exactly when a sender does and doesn't hear about a lost datagram, and build sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission on top of UDP.

warmup.q: A Quarkus service sends a fraud score to a scoring collector as one UDP datagram, and `channel.send()` returns 120, the size of the datagram. What do you know now?
options: The collector received the 120 bytes
The collector's kernel received them, but the collector program may not have read them yet
Your own kernel accepted 120 bytes to send, and nothing more
The datagram left your network card and is on the wire
warmup.why: The return value counts bytes your kernel copied into its own buffer. UDP has no acknowledgment, so nothing ever comes back to confirm delivery: the datagram may be dropped before it leaves your machine, on the way, or in the collector's full receive queue. The second option is tempting because TCP's ACKs tell the sender's kernel that much. UDP says nothing at all.

sections.h: UDP adds ports and a length to IP, and nothing else
sections.body:
Lesson 1 of this track split the transport layer's job in two: pick the right program on the machine (the port), and cope with a network that loses, duplicates and reorders packets (TCP's numbering and resending). What is the least a transport protocol could do? Only the first part. Put a port number on each packet so the receiving kernel knows which program gets it, and leave everything else alone. That protocol exists. It is **UDP**, the User Datagram Protocol, and its specification, RFC 768 from 1980, is three pages long.

Here is a whole UDP datagram from the Try it below: client sends the 16 bytes `AUTH 4242 100.00` to port 9000 on peer. The UDP header in front of them is 8 bytes, four numbers of 16 bits each: source port 52362, destination port 9000, length 24 (8 of header plus 16 of data), and a checksum computed over the header, the data and the two IP addresses, so the receiver can drop a damaged datagram. IP's protocol field says 17, the number lesson 1 listed for UDP.

Count what is missing. There is no handshake, so the first packet already carries data. There is no acknowledgment, so the sender never learns whether anything arrived. Nothing is resent, nothing is put back in order, and duplicates are passed up as they come. The receiver can't ask the sender to slow down, and nothing slows the sender when the network is full. One `send()` becomes one datagram in one IP packet, as long as it fits. A datagram can be up to 65,507 bytes over IPv4, but anything bigger than the path MTU from lesson 4 travels as IP fragments, and losing one fragment loses the whole datagram.

Why would anyone want so little? Because some programs are better off without the rest. A DNS lookup is one question and one answer: a TCP handshake first would triple the round trips. A voice call has no use for a word that arrives a second late, so waiting for a resend is worse than a short gap. A metrics agent sending thousands of counters a second would rather lose a few than slow the service it measures. And protocols that want their own rules start from UDP so the kernel stays out of the way: QUIC, which carries HTTP/3, and the WireGuard VPN both do.

UDP sends nothing back on its own. The one exception comes from the receiving kernel, not from UDP: if no program listens on the destination port, the kernel answers ICMP Port Unreachable, the message traceroute waits for in lesson 4. Whether your program ever hears about that is the subject of the third section.

try.title: Send one datagram and find its header
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab network if it isn't running (`docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d`), then start a UDP echo server on peer with socat: every datagram that arrives on port 9000 goes back to its sender. `ss -uanp` lists UDP sockets: you should see socat on `0.0.0.0:9000`.

Open a shell on client (`docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client bash`) and run the lines below. They send one datagram to the echo server and one to port 9001, where nothing listens, while tcpdump records both. `nc -u` sends each line of input as a UDP datagram.

In the hex of the first datagram, find the UDP header. It starts at byte 34 (`0x22`), right after the `0114` that ends the IP header. Read its four fields. Predict before you look at the end of the output: what does nc's exit code say about the datagram to port 9001?

code.title: first in labs/, then on client
code.src:
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec -d peer socat UDP-RECVFROM:9000,fork SYSTEM:cat
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer ss -uanp

# on client
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn --immediate-mode -w /tmp/udp.pcap 'udp or icmp' 2>/dev/null &
sleep 1
echo -n 'AUTH 4242 100.00' | nc -u -w1 10.10.1.20 9000; echo
echo -n 'AUTH 4242 100.00' | nc -u -w1 10.10.1.20 9001; echo "nc exit code: $?"
sleep 1; kill %1; wait
tcpdump -r /tmp/udp.pcap -nn -XX

try.expect:
From one run (the hex of the later packets trimmed):

```text
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:PortProcess
UNCONN 0      0         127.0.0.11:35553      0.0.0.0:*
UNCONN 0      0            0.0.0.0:9000       0.0.0.0:*    users:(("socat",pid=55,fd=5))

AUTH 4242 100.00
nc exit code: 0
reading from file /tmp/udp.pcap, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144
19:09:00.343049 IP 10.10.1.10.52362 > 10.10.1.20.9000: UDP, length 16
	0x0000:  6edc a299 ec4b 1a77 a5ab e1c1 0800 4500  n....K.w......E.
	0x0010:  002c ccb6 4000 4011 57d9 0a0a 010a 0a0a  .,..@.@.W.......
	0x0020:  0114 cc8a 2328 0018 165b 4155 5448 2034  ....#(...[AUTH.4
	0x0030:  3234 3220 3130 302e 3030                 242.100.00
19:09:00.343118 IP 10.10.1.10.52362 > 10.10.1.20.9000: UDP, length 16
19:09:00.344853 IP 10.10.1.20.9000 > 10.10.1.10.52362: UDP, length 16
19:09:01.349560 IP 10.10.1.10.39785 > 10.10.1.20.9001: UDP, length 16
19:09:01.349696 IP 10.10.1.20 > 10.10.1.10: ICMP 10.10.1.20 udp port 9001 unreachable, length 52
```

The UDP header is `cc8a 2328 0018 165b`: port 52362 (chosen by the kernel), port 9000, length 24, checksum. Byte 23, the IP protocol, is `11`, which is 17. There was no handshake: the first packet already carries `AUTH`. The `127.0.0.11` socket on peer is Docker's built-in DNS server. Toward port 9001, peer's kernel answered Port Unreachable, and nc still exited with 0: it never heard about it. The first datagram shows up twice in this run with the same timestamp to a tenth of a millisecond: the bridge had forgotten which port peer is on, so it flooded the frame, and hairpin mode sent a copy back to client, as in lesson 2. Your run may show it once.

sections.h: A socket is the kernel's mailbox for one port
sections.body:
A program can't put bytes on the wire itself. The network card belongs to the kernel, so the program asks the kernel through a small set of system calls, the **sockets API**. Its design goes back to BSD Unix in 1983, and every language wraps the same calls: C, Kotlin on the JVM, Python, Go.

Build it from what the kernel needs to know. First the program asks for a socket, `socket()`: the kernel creates one, an endpoint for network traffic, and hands back a number the program refers to it by. To receive anything, the socket needs an address, so the program calls `bind()` with an IP address and a port, such as `127.0.0.1:9000`. A socket that sends without binding gets a free port chosen by the kernel at its first send, an ephemeral port (Linux picks from 32768 to 60999). That is where the 52362 in the capture came from. Then `sendto(bytes, address)` hands the kernel one datagram for one destination, and `recvfrom()` waits for one datagram and returns its bytes together with the address it came from. UDP has no `listen()` or `accept()`: one socket can talk to any number of peers, and each datagram says who sent it.

Think of the bound socket as a mailbox the kernel keeps for one port. Datagrams that arrive for port 9000 go into the socket's receive queue, which has a fixed size (`SO_RCVBUF`; Linux's default is 212,992 bytes). Each receive call takes out the oldest datagram, whole. **Message boundaries survive**: three sends become three receives, even if all three are already waiting. That is the opposite of TCP's byte stream from lesson 1, where three writes can come out as one read. The price is that a datagram can't be split across receives. Read one into a buffer that is too small and the rest is cut off and thrown away. So receive into a buffer of 65,535 bytes unless your protocol promises smaller datagrams.

In Kotlin the server side of an echo service is four lines with NIO's `DatagramChannel`:

```kotlin
val channel = DatagramChannel.open().bind(InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 9000))
val buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(65_535)
val from = channel.receive(buffer)   // blocks until one datagram arrives; returns who sent it
channel.send(buffer.flip(), from)    // one datagram back, to that address
```

The older `java.net.DatagramSocket` does the same with `DatagramPacket` objects and has a simple receive timeout, `soTimeout`. A UDP socket can also call `connect()`. Nothing is sent, because there is no connection to make: the kernel only records one peer. After that, `send()` needs no address, datagrams from anyone else are filtered out, and the kernel can report ICMP errors from that peer back to the socket. You will see why that matters in a moment.

try.title: Count receives: UDP against TCP
steps: Start the lab box from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`. It has JDK 25, which runs a single Java file without Gradle.
Read `labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l06/demo/Boundaries.java` first, then predict: how many receives does the UDP part need for three sends, and how many bytes does TCP's single read return?
Run it. On your Mac, `./gradlew :net:demo -Pmain=sfz.net.l06.demo.Boundaries` from the `labs` folder prints the same.
try.expect:
```text
UDP receive 1: 6 bytes "AUTH 1"
UDP receive 2: 7 bytes "AUTH 22"
UDP receive 3: 8 bytes "AUTH 333"
TCP read 1:    21 bytes "AUTH 1AUTH 22AUTH 333"
UDP into a 9-byte buffer: "AUTH 4242" (sent 20 bytes; the other 11 are gone)
```

All three datagrams were waiting in the queue before the first receive, and each receive still returned exactly one. TCP returned the three writes as one run of 21 bytes, with nothing to say where `AUTH 1` ends. The last line is the price of boundaries: a datagram that doesn't fit the buffer is cut, and the rest can't be read later.

sections.h: Nothing tells you a datagram was lost
sections.body:
When `send()` returns on a UDP socket, the kernel has copied your bytes into its own buffer. It doesn't know whether they will leave the machine, and nothing will ever tell it whether they arrived. A datagram can die in three places, and in each one nobody is told.

On the way. A router's queue overflows in a burst, or a Wi-Fi frame is damaged and fails its checksum. The router or the card drops it. In a data centre this is rare. Across the internet some loss is normal, and it comes in bursts when a link is busy.

At the receiver's kernel. If the program doesn't read fast enough, the socket's receive queue fills up, and the kernel drops every new datagram for that socket until there is room again. The queue also counts the kernel's own bookkeeping, not only your bytes. In the Try it below, a socket that asks for a 16 KB queue (Linux doubles a requested `SO_RCVBUF` to leave room for that bookkeeping, so it gets 32 KB) holds just 37 datagrams of 200 bytes: about 900 bytes of queue for each one. The other 1,963 of 2,000 vanish, and the only trace is a counter, `UdpRcvbufErrors`. A 300 ms garbage collection pause in the receiving JVM during a burst does exactly this.

At an empty port. If nothing listens, the receiving kernel answers ICMP Port Unreachable. The sender's kernel gets it, quoting the start of your datagram, but an ordinary UDP socket is never told: it may be talking to a hundred peers, and the kernel doesn't report errors for unconnected sockets. Only a **connected** UDP socket hears it. Its next receive fails with "connection refused", which the JVM turns into `PortUnreachableException`. Even that is a courtesy, not a guarantee, because the ICMP message can be lost or filtered like any other packet.

UDP also doesn't promise order or uniqueness. Datagrams that take different paths can arrive in a different order, and a fault on some link can deliver a copy twice. On one LAN both are rare, which is how bugs that depend on them reach production.

So a UDP program has to decide, for every message, what happens if it disappears. For a metrics counter or a frame of video, the answer is "nothing much". For an authorization request it is not, and the program has to find out by itself. The last section builds that.

try.title: Lose datagrams without a word
steps: In the lab box, read `labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l06/demo/Silence.java`. Part 1 sends to a closed port from an unconnected socket, part 2 does it from a connected `DatagramChannel`, and part 3 sends 2,000 datagrams of 200 bytes to a socket with a 16 KB queue that reads only after the burst.

Predict part 3 before you run it: how many of the 2,000 arrive? Then run it, and ask the kernel's counters what it saw. `nstat -az` prints counters since the box started, so in a fresh box they belong to this run alone.
try.expect:
From one run:

```text
1. send() to closed port 37353 returned normally
   receive(): Receive timed out after 1001 ms
2. connected write() sent 9 bytes
   read(): PortUnreachableException, the ICMP error reached us
3. sent 2000 datagrams, received 37, lost 1963 without a word
#kernel
UdpInDatagrams                  41                 0.0
UdpNoPorts                      2                  0.0
UdpRcvbufErrors                 1963               0.0
```

The same ICMP Port Unreachable came back in parts 1 and 2 (`UdpNoPorts` counts the two datagrams that found no socket), but only the connected channel was told. In part 3 every `send()` succeeded, 37 datagrams fit in the 32 KB queue, and `UdpRcvbufErrors` counted exactly the 1,963 the kernel threw away. On a Mac (run it with Gradle, as in the last Try it) 66 arrived in one run, because macOS sizes the queue differently, and `netstat -s -p udp` counts the rest as `dropped due to full socket buffers`. The exact numbers vary with the machine.

sections.h: Reliability on top of UDP: number, wait, resend, drop duplicates
sections.body:
Suppose your protocol must know that a message arrived. Rebuild what TCP does, one problem at a time.

The receiver says so: it answers every message with an **ACK**. The sender waits for it, but only for a while, because a lost message and a lost ACK look the same from its side: silence. When the wait runs out (the retransmission timeout), it sends the message again. That fixes a lost message, and creates a new problem. If the ACK was the thing that got lost, the receiver now gets the message twice. So every message carries a **sequence number**: 0, 1, 2, and so on. The receiver remembers which numbers it has already handed to the application, delivers each number once, and still ACKs every copy, because a repeat means the sender is still waiting. That is the same idea as an idempotency key on a payment API: a retry carries the same key, and the server does the work once.

What you have now is stop and wait: one message in flight at a time. It is correct, and it is slow. Each message costs at least one round trip, so across 70 ms between US coasts it manages about 14 messages a second, whatever the bandwidth. The fix is to allow many numbered messages in flight at once and to ACK which ones arrived, a window. That is TCP's sliding window, which lessons 7 and 8 open up.

The timeout is the hard part. Too short, and you resend messages that were merely slow, which adds duplicates and load to a network that may already be struggling. Too long, and every loss costs a long pause. TCP measures the round trip time of its own connection and sets the timeout from it (RFC 6298 starts at 1 second), and doubles it after every timeout in a row, so a sender backs off from a congested network instead of hammering it.

Real protocols on UDP do all of this themselves. A DNS client puts a 16-bit ID in its query to match the answer, and asks again after a timeout: dig waits 5 seconds and tries 3 times by default. Repeating a question is harmless, so DNS needs no duplicate check. QUIC (RFC 9000 and RFC 9002) rebuilds everything: packet numbers that are never reused, ACKs that list ranges of received packets, loss detection, congestion control, plus encryption and many streams in one connection. So "UDP is faster than TCP" is true only for the parts you choose to leave out. Once you need reliability, you pay for it either way, and RFC 8085, the IETF's guidelines for applications on UDP, asks you to add congestion control too.

The lab builds the stop-and-wait protocol from the stepper on real UDP sockets, and a relay in the tests drops datagrams on purpose.

stepper.title: A datagram lost with no one noticing, then a retry
stepper.intro: Stop and wait, the simplest reliable protocol on top of UDP: one message in flight, a timer, and a sequence number.

frames.say: 200 ms pass without an ACK. The sender can't tell a lost request from a lost answer or a dead receiver, so it does the one thing that helps in all three cases: it sends the same frame again, with the same sequence number.

try.title: Watch DNS resend over a lossy link
steps: Start a fresh lab box. `tc qdisc ... netem loss 50%` makes the kernel drop half of the packets leaving `eth0`, at random. It affects only this box.
Run six DNS lookups through the lossy link. `+tries=4 +timeout=1` lets dig ask up to four times, waiting one second each time. Predict: how many of the six lookups will fail?
Exit the box when you're done: the loss rule disappears with it.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 50%
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  dig +tries=4 +timeout=1 @1.1.1.1 example.com A +noall +answer +stats | grep -E 'communications error|Query time|^example'
  echo ---
done
tc -s qdisc show dev eth0 | head -2

try.expect:
From one run (the last two lookups, which went through first time, trimmed):

```text
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
example.com.		30	IN	A	172.66.147.243
example.com.		30	IN	A	104.20.23.154
;; Query time: 8 msec
---
example.com.		30	IN	A	104.20.23.154
example.com.		30	IN	A	172.66.147.243
;; Query time: 11 msec
---
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
example.com.		30	IN	A	172.66.147.243
example.com.		30	IN	A	104.20.23.154
;; Query time: 11 msec
---
;; communications error to 1.1.1.1#53: timed out
example.com.		30	IN	A	104.20.23.154
example.com.		30	IN	A	172.66.147.243
;; Query time: 9 msec
---
qdisc netem 8003: root refcnt 13 limit 1000 loss 50%
 Sent 648 bytes 8 pkt (dropped 7, overlimits 0 requeues 0)
```

Every lookup got its answer in the end, because dig resends after its timeout, and every `timed out` line is one lost query and one second of waiting. The third lookup took about 3 seconds, yet dig reports `Query time: 11 msec`, the time of the try that worked. A latency graph built from that number would hide the loss completely. The loss is random, so your run will differ, and with bad luck all four tries of a lookup fail. Neither UDP nor the network told dig anything; it relied on its own timer.

compare.title: The same three messages, read back over UDP and over TCP

a.label: UDP
a.title: three sends, then three receives
a.src:
send("AUTH 1")      receive -> 6 bytes "AUTH 1"
send("AUTH 22")     receive -> 7 bytes "AUTH 22"
send("AUTH 333")    receive -> 8 bytes "AUTH 333"

any of the three may be missing, duplicated or out of order

b.label: TCP
b.title: three writes, then one read
b.src:
write("AUTH 1")
write("AUTH 22")     read -> 21 bytes "AUTH 1AUTH 22AUTH 333"
write("AUTH 333")

all bytes arrive once and in order, with no boundaries

compare.note: Both columns come from `Boundaries.java` in the second Try it. UDP keeps every message whole and separate, and promises nothing about delivery. TCP promises every byte in order, and keeps no message boundaries at all, which is why every protocol on TCP adds its own framing, such as HTTP's `Content-Length` from lesson 1. Neither gives you both, so a protocol on UDP that needs reliability adds sequence numbers and ACKs, and a protocol on TCP that needs messages adds lengths or delimiters.

analogy: UDP is a postcard dropped into a postbox. It needs no envelope and no queue at the counter, and that is why it is quick. You get no receipt, the card can arrive after the one you sent later, and if the recipient's letterbox is already full the postman drops it in the street. Making it reliable means doing the post office's work yourself: number every card, ask the recipient to send a card back for each number, send a copy if no reply comes within a few days, and have the recipient throw away any number it has already read. The analogy breaks on duplicates: a real postal service never delivers the same card twice, while a network occasionally does, so your recipient has to check the numbers even when nothing seems lost.
in_your_world: Two pieces of your payment stack run on UDP without saying so. The first is DNS. A JVM resolving `api.card-issuer.example` sends a UDP query through the C library's resolver, which waits 5 seconds before it asks again (`timeout:5` and `attempts:2` are glibc's defaults in `resolv.conf`). One lost query adds 5 seconds to the first authorization after the JVM's own 30-second DNS cache expires, and nothing in your logs says why. The second is metrics. If your Quarkus services ship Micrometer metrics over StatsD, each counter update is a datagram to an agent on the node. During a traffic spike, the moment you most want accurate numbers, the agent falls behind, its receive queue overflows, and the dashboard undercounts declined authorizations. Watch `UdpRcvbufErrors` (`nstat -az`) on the node, give the agent a larger `SO_RCVBUF`, and keep anything that must not be lost, such as ledger postings and audit events, on TCP or Kafka.
mistake: The common mistake is choosing UDP because "it is faster", and then treating a successful `send()` as delivery. The fast path works perfectly in tests on one machine, where loopback never drops anything. In production, a busy receiver's queue overflows, a router drops a burst, and messages vanish with no exception anywhere. Teams then add a retry, but without sequence numbers, so a lost ACK becomes a duplicate payment or a double-counted event. If you need every message, use TCP or a broker. If you must use UDP, number every message, acknowledge it, retry with a growing timeout, drop duplicates at the receiver, and alert on the kernel's drop counters.

worked.title: Read a UDP datagram by hand

steps.say: The first datagram from the first Try it is 58 bytes. Ethernet takes the first 14, and the IPv4 header starts at byte 14 with `45`. Byte 23, the protocol, is `11` in hex: 17, UDP. Total length `002c` is 44: 20 bytes of IP header and 24 of UDP datagram.
steps.code:
0x0000:  6edc a299 ec4b 1a77 a5ab e1c1 0800 4500
0x0010:  002c ccb6 4000 4011 57d9 0a0a 010a 0a0a
0x0020:  0114 ...

00 2c       total length 44
40 00       Don't Fragment set
40          TTL 64
11          protocol 17: UDP
0a0a 010a   source 10.10.1.10 (client)
0a0a 0114   destination 10.10.1.20 (peer)

steps.say: UDP starts at 14 + 20 = 34. Its header is four 16-bit numbers and nothing else.
steps.code:
0x0020:  0114 cc8a 2328 0018 165b ...

cc 8a   source port 52362, picked by the kernel because nc never called bind()
23 28   destination port 9000, socat's socket
00 18   length 24 = 8 bytes of header + 16 bytes of data
16 5b   checksum over the header, the data and both IP addresses

steps.say: The data starts at 34 + 8 = 42 and runs to the end of the frame: exactly what `echo -n` gave nc, with no length prefix and no terminator. The receiving kernel doesn't need one, because the UDP length field already says where the message ends.

Compare the reply from peer. The ports have swapped places and the data is the same. Nothing in either header numbers the datagram or acknowledges the other one: if the protocol needs that, it has to be inside the 16 bytes of data, which is what the lab's `Frame` does with 5 bytes of its own header.
steps.code:
reply: 10.10.1.20.9000 > 10.10.1.10.52362: UDP, length 16

23 28   source port 9000
cc 8a   destination port 52362
00 18   length 24

the lab's frame inside the data: 01 byte kind | 4 bytes seq | message

lab.title: A UDP echo server, and a reliability layer that survives loss
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 13 fail. They use real UDP sockets on 127.0.0.1 and no Docker. `Frame.kt` is finished: 1 byte for DATA or ACK, 4 bytes of sequence number, then the message.

In `UdpEcho.kt`, write `UdpEchoServer.serve` (receive, flip, send back, until the channel closes) and `udpRequest` (one datagram out, one back, or null after the timeout). Run `UdpEchoTest` until its 6 tests pass.
In `Reliable.kt`, write `ReliableReceiver.handle`: deliver the expected sequence number once, count older ones as duplicates, and ACK both.
Write `ReliableSender.send`: send DATA, wait for the matching ACK, resend on timeout, give up after `maxAttempts`.

Read `src/test/kotlin/sfz/net/l06/LossyLink.kt`: a relay between sender and receiver that drops chosen datagrams. The tests lose the first DATA, the first ACK, and then every third datagram one way and every fourth the other. Run the tests until all 13 pass.
hints: `channel.receive(buffer)` throws `AsynchronousCloseException` when `close()` runs on another thread. It is a `ClosedChannelException`, so one `catch` ends the loop.
In `udpRequest`, `DatagramSocket().use { ... }` closes the socket for you. Return `packet.data.copyOf(packet.length)`: the buffer is bigger than the datagram.
In `send`, keep the sequence number in a local variable and only advance `nextSeq` after the right ACK. A stale ACK means "keep waiting", not "try again".
To wait the rest of one timeout after a stale ACK, compute a deadline with `System.nanoTime()` and set `socket.soTimeout` to what is left before each `receive`.
In `handle`, send the ACK for every DATA with `seq <= expected` after you update `expected`. A DATA from the future (`seq > expected`) can't happen in stop and wait; ignore it.

drill.title: Write the stop-and-wait sender from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the body of `send(message)` for a stop-and-wait sender over a `DatagramSocket`: frame the message with the next sequence number, send it, wait for the matching ACK with a timeout, resend on timeout, give up after a fixed number of attempts. Then say in one sentence what the receiver must do with a DATA frame whose sequence number it has already delivered.

recap: UDP adds an 8-byte header to IP: source port, destination port, length and checksum. No handshake, no ACK, no resend, no ordering, no flow or congestion control.
A socket is the kernel's mailbox for one port. Each send is one datagram and each receive returns exactly one, whole; a buffer that's too small cuts it.
`send()` succeeding means only that your kernel took the bytes. Datagrams die on the way, in a full receive queue (counted in `UdpRcvbufErrors`), or at a closed port.
Only a connected UDP socket hears about ICMP Port Unreachable, as `PortUnreachableException` in the JVM. An unconnected one hears nothing.
Reliability on UDP means sequence numbers, ACKs, a retransmission timeout and dropping duplicates. DNS does a little of it; QUIC rebuilds all of TCP's work.

quiz.q: A service sends one 1,000-byte UDP datagram per payment event to a log collector. During a burst the collector's JVM pauses for garbage collection for 300 ms. What happens to the datagrams that arrive during the pause?
options: They wait in the network until the collector reads again
The collector's kernel queues what fits in the socket's receive buffer and drops the rest; the sender is not told
The collector's kernel tells the sender to slow down, and the sender's `send()` blocks
They are delivered later, out of order, but all of them arrive
quiz.why: The network doesn't hold packets for a slow program, and UDP has no flow control to push back on the sender. The receiving kernel keeps what fits in the socket's queue and drops the rest, counting it in `UdpRcvbufErrors`. The sender's `send()` calls all succeeded. Blocking the sender is what TCP's flow control would do, and UDP has none.

quiz.q: A client sends three datagrams of 100, 200 and 300 bytes to a server that reads with a 1,000-byte buffer. What can the server's receive calls return?
options: Receives of exactly 100, 200 and 300 bytes, one datagram each, for those that arrive
One receive of 600 bytes, if all three arrived before it read
Any split of the 600 bytes, depending on the MTU
Three receives of 1,000 bytes, padded with zeros
quiz.why: UDP keeps message boundaries: each receive returns one whole datagram. Some may be lost and they may come in another order, but they are never merged or split. Merging bytes into one read is TCP's byte stream, the habit this question tests.

quiz.q: A `DatagramChannel` is connected to `10.10.1.20:9001`, where nothing listens. It writes a datagram, then calls `read()`. What happens, assuming nothing filters ICMP?
options: `read()` blocks forever, since UDP never gets answers
`write()` throws `ConnectException`
`read()` throws `PortUnreachableException`, because the kernel passes the ICMP Port Unreachable to the connected socket
`read()` returns 0 bytes
quiz.why: The peer's kernel answers with ICMP Port Unreachable. Because the socket is connected, your kernel knows which socket it is about and reports it on the next operation, which the JVM turns into `PortUnreachableException`. An unconnected socket would hear nothing and `read()` would wait for its timeout. `write()` succeeds either way, because nothing is known yet when it runs.

quiz.q: In a stop-and-wait protocol over UDP, the receiver gets DATA with sequence number 7, which it has already delivered. What should it do?
options: Drop it silently: it is a duplicate
Deliver it again, since the sender clearly wants it delivered
Send a negative acknowledgment so the sender stops
Send ACK 7 again without delivering it
quiz.why: A repeat means the sender never got the first ACK 7, so it will keep resending until one arrives. Dropping it silently makes the sender retry until it gives up, and delivering it again would authorize a payment twice. ACK again, deliver once.

quiz.q: From lesson 4: the ICMP Port Unreachable a UDP sender gets back quotes the start of the datagram it is about. Which quoted fields let the sender's kernel find the socket the error belongs to?
options: Only the ICMP checksum
The quoted IP addresses and the first 8 bytes after the IP header, which hold the UDP source and destination ports
The whole data of the datagram, which the kernel compares with recent sends
The TTL, which is unique per socket
quiz.why: Every ICMP error quotes the dead packet's IP header plus at least 8 more bytes. For UDP, those 8 bytes are the whole UDP header, so the kernel has the addresses and both ports, enough to find the socket. Traceroute uses the same quote to match answers to its probes by port.

flashcards.front: The four fields of the UDP header?
flashcards.back: Source port, destination port, length (header plus data), checksum. 16 bits each, 8 bytes in all.

flashcards.front: What does a successful UDP `send()` tell you?
flashcards.back: That your own kernel accepted the bytes. Nothing about whether they left the machine or arrived.

flashcards.front: What happens when you receive a UDP datagram into a buffer that is too small?
flashcards.back: You get the first bytes and the rest is thrown away. Receive into 65,535 bytes unless your protocol promises smaller datagrams.

flashcards.front: Where does Linux count UDP datagrams it dropped because a socket's queue was full?
flashcards.back: `UdpRcvbufErrors`, shown by `nstat -az` (or `netstat -su` as receive buffer errors).
It fixes one peer: send needs no address, other senders are filtered out, and ICMP errors such as Port Unreachable are reported to the socket (`PortUnreachableException` in the JVM).

flashcards.front: The four parts of a minimal reliability layer on UDP?
flashcards.back: Sequence numbers, ACKs, a retransmission timeout, and a receiver that delivers each number once but ACKs every copy.

flashcards.front: Why is stop and wait slow?
flashcards.back: One message per round trip: at 70 ms RTT, about 14 messages a second, whatever the bandwidth. Windows (many in flight) fix it.

terms.plain: One self-contained UDP message, sent and received whole.
The kernel's endpoint for one conversation or port, which a program reads and writes through system calls.
A free port the kernel picks for a socket that never called `bind()`.
The socket's queue of arrived datagrams (`SO_RCVBUF`); when it is full, new ones are dropped.
A UDP socket fixed to one peer, which also receives that peer's ICMP errors.
A number on each message so the receiver can spot duplicates and order.
How long a sender waits for an ACK before it sends the message again.
A protocol that keeps one message in flight and sends the next only after its ACK.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate proposes sending ledger postings from one service to another over UDP, "because it's faster and the network never drops anything here". Explain what UDP does and doesn't do, where postings could disappear, and what you would have to build to make it safe.
explain_back.answer: UDP only puts ports, a length and a checksum on a datagram. There's no handshake, no acknowledgment and no resend, so a successful send only means our own kernel took the bytes. A posting can vanish in a router queue during a burst, in the receiver's socket queue when the receiving service pauses or falls behind, which the kernel only counts in UdpRcvbufErrors, or at a closed port during a deploy, where only a connected socket would even hear about it. A copy can also arrive twice. To make it safe we would number every posting, have the receiver acknowledge each one, resend after a timeout that backs off, and have the receiver apply each number once while acknowledging every copy, which is the idempotency-key idea. Then we'd want many postings in flight for speed, and congestion control so retries don't swamp the network. At that point we've rebuilt TCP, so for postings I'd use TCP or Kafka and keep UDP for data we can afford to lose, like metrics.

deeper.body:
**One thread per UDP socket isn't enough.** A UDP server has one socket for all its clients, so one thread reading it becomes the bottleneck. On Linux, `SO_REUSEPORT` lets several sockets bind the same port, and the kernel spreads datagrams across them by hashing the addresses and ports, so each thread gets its own socket and queue. DNS servers and QUIC servers use it.

**How big should a datagram be?** Stay under the path MTU from lesson 4 and the datagram travels as one packet; go over and IP fragments it, and losing any fragment loses all of it. DNS learned this the hard way: since DNS Flag Day 2020, resolvers advertise EDNS buffers of 1,232 bytes, small enough to fit an IPv6 packet of 1,280 bytes without fragments, and anything bigger moves to TCP. Platforms also cap datagram sizes: macOS refuses to send UDP datagrams over 9,216 bytes by default (`net.inet.udp.maxdgram`), which is why this lesson's lab tests stop at 8,000 bytes.

**Why QUIC lives in user space.** TCP is in the kernel, so improving it means waiting years for every operating system to update. QUIC runs on UDP inside the application or its library, so a browser or a server can ship a new congestion controller with its next release. The cost is CPU: the kernel's UDP path was built for small datagrams, so Linux added UDP segmentation offload (GSO) and receive offload (GRO), which pass many datagrams through the stack as one.

**Java details.** `DatagramChannel` can be non-blocking and registered with a `Selector`, so one thread can serve many sockets. Since JDK 15 the old `DatagramSocket` is implemented on top of `DatagramChannel` (JEP 373), so both behave the same underneath. Virtual threads work with blocking UDP calls too.
